prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Still, citizen sparrow, this vulture which you call Unnatural, let him but lumber again to air Over the rotten office, let him bear The carrion ballast up, and at the tall Tip of the sky lie cruising. Then you’ll see That no more beautiful bird is in heaven’s height, No wider more placid wings, no watchfuller flight; He shoulders nature there, the frightfully free, The naked-headed one. Pardon him, you Who dart in the orchard aisles, for it is he Devours death, mocks mutability, Has heart to make an end, keeps nature new. Thinking of Noah, childheart, try to forget How for so many bedlam hours his saw Soured the song of birds with its wheezy gnaw, And the slam of his hammer all the day beset The people’s ears. Forget that he could bear To see the towns like coral under the keel, And the fields so dismal deep. Try rather to feel How high and weary it was, on the waters where He rocked his only world, and everyone’s. Forgive the hero, you who would have died Gladly with all you knew; he rode that tide To Ararat; all men are Noah’s sons.

Keywords: Still, Unnatural, Over

outputs.L1:
Still, citizen sparrow, consider this vulture you call unnatural:  
Let him but lumber once again into the air  
Above the rotting office; let him bear  
His carrion ballast upward and, at the tall  
Tip of the sky, lie cruising. Then you will see  
That no more beautiful bird inhabits heaven’s height—  
No wings wider or more placid, no flight more watchful.  
He shoulders nature there: the frightfully free,  
The naked-headed one. Pardon him, you  
Who dart among the orchard aisles, for it is he  
Who devours death, mocks mutability,  
Has the heart to make an end, and keeps nature new.

Thinking of Noah, child-heart, try to forget  
How, for so many bedlam hours, his saw  
Soured the birdsong with its wheezing gnaw,  
And how the pounding of his hammer all day beset  
The people’s ears. Forget that he could bear  
To see the towns like coral beneath the keel,  
And the fields submerged in dismal depths. Try instead to feel  
How high and weary he was upon the waters, where  
He rocked his only world—and everyone’s.  
Forgive the hero, you who would have died  
Gladly with all you knew; he rode that tide  
To Ararat. All men are Noah’s sons.
outputs.L2:
Yet, little sparrow of the common world, allow the vulture you condemn as unnatural to heave himself once more above his foul occupation. Let him lift his burden of dead flesh and circle near the summit of the heavens. There you will discover that the sky holds no lovelier bird: none has broader, calmer wings or a more vigilant course. Bald and terrifyingly unrestrained, he bears nature upon his shoulders. Forgive him, orchard-dweller, swift among the rows of trees, because he consumes what is dead, defies decay, possesses the courage to finish things, and continually renews the natural world.

And when you think of Noah, tenderhearted child, set aside the memory of those many maddening hours when his rasping saw spoiled the birds’ music and his hammer’s blows tormented every ear from morning to night. Forget that he endured the sight of towns submerged like coral beneath his vessel and fields buried beneath bleak depths. Think instead of his exhaustion and isolation, rocking high upon the flood while carrying the only world left to him—the world belonging to everyone. You who would willingly have perished beside everything familiar, pardon the hero who traveled across those waters until he reached Ararat. Every human being descends from Noah.
outputs.L3:
The speaker urges the “citizen sparrow” to reconsider its judgment of the vulture. Although the bird may appear awkward and ungainly while walking on land, it becomes majestic once it takes flight. Its true value lies not in its appearance but in its essential role within nature. By feeding on carrion, the vulture “devours death”: it confronts decay directly, clears away what has died, and helps make renewal possible.

The poem extends this call for understanding to Noah. Readers are asked to forgive him for the disruption caused by building the ark and even for surviving while towns, fields, and familiar ways of life disappeared beneath the floodwaters. Noah’s burden was immense and profoundly lonely, since the ark carried not only his own life but his entire world and the future of humanity. Others might have preferred to perish alongside everything they had known rather than endure such isolation and loss. Yet Noah’s willingness to survive transformed him into a hero, for through him human life continued. He therefore became, in the poem’s vision, the ancestor of all humanity.
outputs.L4:
The poem asks readers to reconsider figures whose actions initially appear unnatural, cruel, or morally troubling. It focuses on the carrion-eating vulture and the biblical figure of Noah, placing them side by side as agents of destruction and renewal. On the surface, both are associated with death: the vulture tears into decaying bodies, while Noah survives a flood that destroys nearly all life outside the ark. Yet the poem suggests that judging either figure only by these disturbing images overlooks the larger purpose each serves.

The vulture’s behavior may seem ugly because it feeds on the dead, but its role in nature is essential. By consuming carrion, it clears away decay and helps return dead matter to the cycle of life. Its apparent violence is therefore not pointless or malicious. Instead, the bird performs necessary work that other creatures avoid. The poem finds an unexpected beauty in this function, presenting the vulture as a figure willing to confront death directly so that the living world can continue.

Noah occupies a similarly complicated position. Although he is traditionally remembered as a righteous survivor and rescuer, his story is inseparable from catastrophe. He preserves his family and the animals in the ark, but he does so while the old world is being erased by the flood. His heroism lies not in preventing loss, which is beyond his power, but in carrying the possibility of life through destruction. Like the vulture, Noah stands at the boundary between death and renewal.

By connecting these two figures, the poem challenges conventional ideas about beauty, goodness, and heroism. What appears cruel may be necessary, and what appears repulsive may contribute to survival. Renewal does not occur without the removal of what has died or can no longer endure. Preservation likewise requires courage from those willing to face devastation rather than turn away from it.

Ultimately, the poem presents destruction and creation as closely connected forces. The vulture cleanses the earth through consumption, while Noah protects the seeds of a future world amid overwhelming loss. Both reveal that survival depends on agents capable of confronting death, accepting change, and transforming ruin into the possibility of new life.
outputs.L5:
The room was still, holding its breath beneath the pale morning light. Everything looked familiar, yet somehow unnatural—the chairs too straight, the silence too complete, the clock frozen between seconds.

She stood by the window and watched the empty street. It was over; she knew that now. There would be no final explanation, no sudden return, no voice calling her name.

And yet, as the sun rose above the rooftops, the world began moving again. Slowly, reluctantly, she moved with it.
